title: Composition regulation and defects introduction via amorphous CuEu alloy shell for efficient CO2 electroreduction toward methane
abstract: Cu is considered as a promising catalyst for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (ECO2RR) into useful chemicals/fuels, such as CH4. However, its poor selectivity and low activity toward target products remain urgent issues. Here, novel core/shell Cu@CuEu nanoparticles (NPs) with amorphous CuEu alloy shell synthesized via a simple co-reduction method were used as cathodes for ECO2RR in KHCO3 aqueous solution. The CH4 Faradaic efficiency of the optimized Cu@CuEu NPs was 74.7 %, which was 3.4-fold higher than that of Cu NPs. Moreover, the Cu@CuEu NPs exhibited a high current density of 45.4 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The amorphous CuEu shell triggered the reaction via a synergistic effect between electronic structure regulation and abundant active defective sites, thus facilitating highly efficient methane production from CO2 electroreduction.

A B S T R A C T
Cu is considered as a promising catalyst for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (ECO2RR) into useful chemicals/fuels, such as CH4. However, its poor selectivity and low activity toward target products remain urgent issues. Here, novel core/shell Cu@CuEu nanoparticles (NPs) with amorphous CuEu alloy shell synthesized via a simple co-reduction method were used as cathodes for ECO2RR in KHCO3 aqueous solution. The CH4 Faradaic efficiency of the optimized Cu@CuEu NPs was 74.7 %, which was 3.4-fold higher than that of Cu NPs. Moreover, the Cu@CuEu NPs exhibited a high current density of 45.4 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The amorphous CuEu shell triggered the reaction via a synergistic effect between electronic structure regulation and abundant active defective sites, thus facilitating highly efficient methane production from CO2 electroreduction.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical conversion of CO2 into value-added chemicals is an ideal route to curb increased atmospheric CO2 levels. However, this process suffers from several important problems, such as high cost, many different products, and low efficiency. Therefore, the design of new electrocatalysts with adequate activity and product selectivity for driving the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (ECO2RR) is essential [1–5]. As transition-metal electrocatalysts, Cu electrodes have the unique capability to reduce CO2 into hydrocarbon products and are highly cost-effective and nontoxic materials [6]. However, they have the disadvantages of wide product distribution and low activity that limit their further industrial application [7]. Therefore, the optimization of Cu-based electrocatalysts is crucial to improve the activity and selectivity of specific reduction products.
CH4 formation via ECO2RR involves an eight-electron transfer process on Cu-based electrocatalysts and is accompanied by the acquisition of other products, such as CO (2 electrons), HCOOH (2 electrons), and C2H4 (16 electrons) [8]. In addition, in aqueous solutions, ECO2RR is considerably hindered by side reactions with the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), causing poor of CH4 selectivity. Theoretical studies have proposed that some intermediates (*CO, *CHO, or *COH) must efficiently bind with Cu
surfaces in the electroreduction of CO2 into CH4 [9]. Several approaches, such as tuning electrocatalyst morphologies [10], particle size [11], alloying [12], and crystal facets [13], have been proven to be promising strategies for enhancing CH4 selectivity in ECO2RR. Among these methods, metal alloying has proven to be a reliable approach for efficient CO2 reduction due to its electronic and geometric effects, which can effectively regulate the binding energy of intermediates to facilitate CH4 selectivity on catalyst surfaces [14–16]. For example, a concave rhombic dodecahedral Cu3Pd with enriched low-coordinated sites and composition effects that was synthesized via a facile one-pot approach exhibits high selectivity for CH4 [17]. Zhang et al. reported that Cu2Pd nanoalloy particles on the surfaces of polymeric films are favorable for tuning intermediate binding strength to achieve a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 51 % in CH4 production in ionic liquid [18]. However, the extranuclear electron configurations of representative transition metals adopted in most Cu-based alloying methods are similar to those of Cu. Rare-earth elements have attracted special interest as foreign metals for modulating the catalytic properties of various metals because of the unique electronic and chemical properties of their 4f0−14 subshell electron configuration [19,20], which are different from those of transition metals. The use of rare earth metals for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 on Cu-based alloy electrocatalysts has rarely been reported.

As-synthesized core/shell Cu@CuEu NPs with different thicknesses of amorphous CuEu shells were fabricated by tuning different proportions of Eu/Cu precursors during the particle formation process. In 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte saturated with CO2, the optimized Cu@CuEu NPs exhibited excellent ECO2RR activity with CH4 and suppressed the formation of other products. The drastically altered catalytic performance of the NPs was confirmed through X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES), and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements. The results of these analyses suggested that the introduction of Eu into Cu optimized electronic structure and resulted in the formation of abundant active defective sites in amorphous CuEu alloy.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Eu(NO3)3·6H2O (99 %) and triethylene glycol (TEG) (99 %) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical. Cu(CH3COO)2 (98 %) was purchased from Alorich. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP K30) was purchased from BASF of Germany. CH3COCH3 and CH3CH2OH were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical. All the chemicals were used without further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Synthesis of Cu@CuEu NPs
sections.text: A total of 1 mL of TEG containing 0.18 mmol Cu(CH3COO)2 was dissolved into 1 mL of TEG containing 0.02 mmol Eu(NO3)3·6H2O and 22.2 mg of PVP K30 at room temperature. After dissolution, the two solutions were mixed evenly to form a homogeneous mixed solution. In a 50 mL threenecked flask, 22.2 mg of PVP K30 powder was dissolved in 20 mL of TEG at room temperature. Next, the above-mentioned solution was heated to 260 °C. Then, the mixed homogeneous solution was quickly injected into a flask with strong magnetic stirring. After maintenance at this temperature for 10 min, the whole reactor was cooled down quickly. The resulting purple solution was washed with acetone and ethanol and centrifuged (10,000 rpm for 10 min) several times to obtain a black precipitate. The precipitate was dried in a vacuum-drying oven for 12 h to obtain a dry powder. The above-mentioned sample was the core/shell Cu@CuEu-1 NPs, where “1” represents Eu/Cu precursor ratios starting at 1:9. For comparison, different as-synthesized samples were prepared by changing the molar feed ratio of Eu/Cu (Table S1) under identical conditions and denoted as Cu@CuEu-2 NPs and Cu@CuEu-3 NPs.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Synthesis of Cu NPs
sections.text:
The synthesis process of Cu NPs was similar to that of the core/shell Cu/CuEu NPs with the omission of Eu from the solution. A total of 1 mL of TEG containing 0.2 mmol Cu(CH3COO)2 and 22.2 mg of PVP K30 was
dissolved to form a homogeneous mixed solution at room temperature. In a 50 mL flask, 22.2 mg of PVP K30 powder was dissolved in 20 mL of TEG at room temperature. Next, the above-mentioned solution was heated to 260 °C. Then, the mixed homogeneous solution was quickly injected into a flask under vigorous stirring. After stirring for another 10 min, a red solid powder was obtained after washing, centrifuging several times with acetone and ethanol, and vacuum drying.

sections.heading: 2.3. Preparation of the working electrode
sections.text: Working electrodes were prepared via a simple method. A total of 8 μL of homogeneous ink, which was prepared by using 5 mg of carbonsupported nanoparticle catalysts (the prepared catalyst (1.0 mg) and carbon black (4.0 mg)) dispersed in absolute ethanol (950 μL) and 5 wt % Nafion solution (50 μL) with ultrasonic mixing for 30 min. The ink was dropped onto a glassy carbon electrode with an effective diameter of 5 mm and dried under natural conditions.

sections.heading: 2.4. Physical characterizations
sections.text:
The powder XRD patterns of the samples were obtained on a Bruker AXS D5000 diffractometer with Cu Ka radiation (λ =1.5405 nm). The morphologies of the samples were recorded by using TEM on a Tecnai G2 F30 electron microscope with an accelerating voltage of 300 kV. The metal content of the catalysts was quantified via ICP–OES (Optima 8300). XPS measurements were performed on a PHI 5700 system by using a 200 W monochromatic Al X-ray source. Typically, the hydrocarbon C1s line at 284.8 eV from adventitious carbon was used for energy referencing. The chemical state changes of each Cu electrode were further obtained by using
XANES in the BL08U1A beamline at the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics, China. Cu L-edge XANES was performed over the energy regions of 920–960 eV.

sections.heading: 2.5. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text: A standard three-electrode cell arrangement equipped with an electrochemical workstation (CHI 760 E, Shanghai CH Instruments Co., China) was used to perform the electrochemical experiments. The electrodes consisted of a cathode (working electrode), an anode (platinum gauze counter electrode), and a reference electrode (Ag/AgCl (3.5 M KCl)). A single-compartment batch cell with a H-type electrolytic cell was separated by a Nafion 117 proton exchange membrane and filled with 20 mL of 0.5 M NaHCO3 aqueous solution (pH = 7.2). Highpurity CO2 gas was used to purge the cathodic compartment at a rate of 20.00 sccm for approximately 30 min. All measured potentials were converted into RHE by using the formula E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.209 V + 0.0591 V × pH. ECSAs were analyzed through CV measurements in the non-Faradaic processes over a potential range and are linearly related to the Cdl of supported Cu NPs and Cu@CuEu-X NPs.

sections.heading: 2.6. Analysis of electrolysis products
sections.text:
For gas product analysis, a gas chromatograph equipped with a thermal conductivity detector and flame ionization detector was used.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Core/shell Cu@CuEu NPs were synthesized via one-step reduction by using TEG solution as a reductant and solvent and PVP K30 as a surfactant. A detailed description of the synthesis method is provided in the Experimental Section. Three kinds of Cu@CuEu NPs that were denoted as Cu@CuEu-1 NPs, Cu@CuEu-2 NPs, and Cu@CuEu-3 NPs were prepared by controlling Eu/Cu precursor ratios at 1:9, 1:4, and 1:1 (Table S1), respectively. The metal contents of core/shell Cu@CuEu NPs were analyzed via inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP–OES). The bulk Eu/Cu ratios of the NPs were 0.052:1, 0.109:1, and 0.571:1 (Table S2). The atomic ratios of surface Eu/Cu for Cu@CuEu-1 NPs, Cu@CuEu-2 NPs, and Cu@CuEu-3 NPs collected through XPS were 0.50:1, 0.86:1, and 1.82:1 (Table S3), respectively. These results showed that three kinds of Cu@CuEu NPs with different shell contents were obtained by using the synthesis method reported here.
The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images presented in Figures S1 and S2 clearly show that the as-synthesized Cu@CuEu NPs had a diameter of approximately 100 nm, which was the same as the diameter of Cu NPs. As displayed in Figs. 1a and S1, the three core/shell Cu@CuEu NPs
possessed amorphous shells and exhibited good dispersion. In addition, the thickness of the amorphous shells consistently increased with the change in Eu/Cu precursor ratios. The energy-dispersive X-ray spectrum shown in Figure S3 clearly confirms the presence of elemental Cu and Eu. The EDX elemental mappings of CuEu-1 NPs in Fig. 2c show a clearly defined core/ shell structure with Cu (yellow) centered in the core and a shell that was composed of disordered Cu and Eu (green). This result was also further supported by EDX line scans (Figure S4). The lattice fringes of the crystalline structure in the core area displayed interplanar spacings of 0.209 nm, which matched well with the (111) plane of metallic Cu as shown in Fig. 1b and by high resolution-transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM). Furthermore, the peaks in the X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra (Fig. 1d) can be assigned to the (111), (200), and (220) planes of fcc Cu (JCPDS No. 04-0836). The peak position of the three Cu@CuEu NPs did not shift distinctly relative to that of Cu NPs. However, crystallinity decreased with the increase in amorphous shell thickness. This result further suggested that the bimetallic nanostructures were composed of crystallized Cu and amorphous EuCu alloy.
In addition, the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA), which is positively linearly related with double-layer capacitance (Cdl), was analyzed to elucidate the effect of the amorphous CuEu alloy shells of Cu@CuEu NPs on ECO2RR. As shown in Figure S7, the cyclic voltammogram (CV) curves of Cu NPs and Cu@CuEu NPs from 0.8 V to 1.0 V vs. RHE at different potentials were obtained by calculating double-layer charging currents. The reduction current density at −0.9 V vs. RHE plotted against scan rate is shown in Fig. 3d. The slope of the straight line was the Cdl of electrocatalysis. Cu@CuEu NPs had a larger slope than Cu NPs. The increase in active sites might be attributed to abundant defects on the amorphous shells
and enhanced the efficiency of ECO2RR [29,30]. The durability of Cu@CuEu-1 NPs was tested at −1.2 V vs. RHE for 120 min. The FE of CH4 slightly decreased during electrolysis (Figure S8). As shown in Figure S9, Eu spillover was notable in Cu@CuEu-1 NPs after electrolysis, indicating that CH4 activity was affected by the CuEu alloy in the shell.
Electronic structure plays a key role in the activity of heterogeneous catalysts [31]. The surface chemical compositions of Cu NPs and the three Cu@CuEu NPs were determined via XPS. The results provided in Figure S10 clearly reveal the presence of Cu and Eu elements on the three Cu@CuEu NPs. Fig. 3a shows that the Cu 2p spectra of Cu NPs and Cu@CuEu-X NPs could be fitted into four dominant peaks that corresponded to Cu2+ (2p1/2, 953.5 and 2p3/2, 933.9 eV) and Cu1+/0 (2p1/2, 951.8 and 2p3/2, 932.1 eV) [32]. Other small peaks could be attributed to satellite peaks. Meanwhile, the as-synthesized Cu@CuEu NPs showed the presence of weak peaks that were associated with the spectral doublets Eu 3d3/2 and Eu 3d5/2 at 1143 and 1135 eV, respectively (Fig. 3b). Notably, the BEs of Cu2+ and Cu1+/0 peaks for the three Cu@CuEu NPs had shifted by ∼0.15 eV compared with that of Cu NPs. The slight red shifts in the binding energies of Cu@CuEu-2 NPs and Cu@CuEu-3 NPs relative to the peaks of Cu@CuEu-1 NPs indicated that the introduction of Eu changed the electronic structure of Cu, further confirming the formation of CuEu alloy. In addition, the relative intensity ratio of Cu2+/Cu1+/0 increased with the increase in Eu content (Table S4). These phenomena were indicative of strong electronic interaction between Cu and Eu that was conducive to tuning the binding energy between intermediates and Cu [17].
The variation in the local atomic/electronic structure of Cu on the
amorphous CuEu alloy shell was measured by analyzing the Cu L3-edge XANES spectra of Cu NPs and Cu@CuEu-X NPs (Fig. 3c). The as-synthesized samples exhibited the Cu L3 absorption peak at ∼932 eV [33]. The two characteristic peaks at 930 and 933 eV could be assigned to Cu2+ and Cu1+, respectively. The Cu2+ and Cu1+/0 peaks of Cu@CuEu NPs clearly shifted to higher BEs relative to those of Cu NPs. These results were in accordance with the above XPS results, confirming that charge transfer occurred between Cu and Eu within the alloy shells. The area under resonances (integral calculation of the absorption region) was proportional to the amount of the d-character’s unoccupied density of states (DOS) [34]. As can be clearly seen in Figure S11, compared with that for Cu NPs, the number of Cu-unoccupied DOS for Cu@CuEu-1 NPs increased. However, for Cu@CuEu-2 NPs and Cu@CuEu-3 NPs, the number of Cu- unoccupied DOS decreased significantly. This phenomenon indicated that a small amount of Eu content in the CuEu amorphous shell might help the electron transfer of Cu.
Cu NPs and Cu@CuEu-1 NPs were subjected to EPR analysis to further probe the chemical environment of the amorphous CuEu shell. The results are shown in Fig. 3d. In contrast to Cu NPs, Cu@CuEu-1 NPs exhibited the obvious peak of g = 2.003, which is a typical characteristic of oxygen vacancies (Vo). This result clearly indicated that the addition of Eu was conducive to the introduction of point defects and the localization of free electrons [35]. Electronic structure and EPR analysis results proved that core/shell Cu@CuEu NPs possessed well-defined CuEu alloy shell with localized electron characteristics. The above analytical results indicated that the enhanced activity and selectivity of CH4 for Cu@CuEu-1 NPs could be
ascribed to the interaction between Cu–Eu (higher oxygen affinity) and abundant point defects on the amorphous alloy shell (as illustrated in Fig. 4). Although the optimized CuEu alloy shell could affect the distribution of the electron valence state content of Cu, increase activity sites, and introduce point defects, the excess Eu content of the amorphous CuEu shell might hinder the effective binding of the CO2 intermediate to Cu, thus leading to HER.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, core/shell Cu@CuEu NPs with amorphous CuEu alloy shell were synthesized via a controllable co-reduction method. The thicknesses of the amorphous shells of core/shell Cu@CuEu NPs could be easily adjusted through the regulation of compositional ratio. The Cu@CuEu-1 NPs were highly active and selective electrocatalysts for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 into CH4. The FE and current density of CH4 could reach as high as 45.4 mA cm−2 and 74.7 % at −1.2 V vs. RHE, respectively. The superior performance of the electrocatalysts originated mainly from the electronic-regulating effect between Cu and Eu and abundant active defective sites in the CuEu amorphous shell. Our work is helpful for guiding the design of highly efficient Cu-based alloy ECO2RR electrocatalysts.
